item.title: Anthropic blocks users for activities related to training larger models, including research automation and fine-tuning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Researcher Jiahao Shao criticized Anthropic for blocking his access after he used their Claude model to submit jobs and run analysis related to training larger AI models. Shao said his work did not involve distilling Claude but was flagged as "training a competitor," leading to downgrades and session terminations. He expressed frustration that Anthropic, which built its models on global data, treats paying users conducting research automation as adversaries.

item.title: Researchers bypass ChatGPT sandbox to execute JavaScript in user sessions, enabling account takeover via shared conversation links, fixed by OpenAI in October 2026 [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: A research team discovered a vulnerability in ChatGPT's sharing feature that allowed attackers to execute JavaScript within the signed-in sessions of users who opened maliciously crafted shared conversation links. This exploit enabled attackers to access private conversations and perform actions as the victim without requiring any additional user interaction beyond opening the link. The issue stemmed from a combination of ChatGPT's HTML Preview feature and a math library called MathLive, which improperly handled cross-origin messages, allowing code execution in the main ChatGPT page. The researchers detailed how the Preview feature ran code in a restricted frame, but the MathLive library installed a message listener on the main page that accepted unverified messages, enabling the injection of malicious HTML and JavaScript. OpenAI addressed the vulnerability on October 26, 2026, classifying it as a high-priority (P1) security issue. The report highlights the risks of combining seemingly harmless features without adequate security checks, leading to a critical account takeover vector.

item.title: Bloomberg reports computer science degree programs see declining enrollment as AI automation reduces job opportunities [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Computer science degree programs are experiencing a drop in student enrollment as advances in artificial intelligence automate tasks traditionally performed by human workers. This trend reflects growing concerns about the future job market for graduates in the field. The decline in interest in computer science studies is linked to AI's increasing ability to replace roles in software development and related areas, prompting students to reconsider career prospects in technology sectors. Educational institutions are facing challenges in adapting to these shifts and attracting new students amid changing industry demands.

item.title: DeepSeek publishes architecture for always-on autonomous coding agent on GitHub as a research prototype [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: DeepSeek has released the architecture for its always-on autonomous coding agent, dsh-superagent, on GitHub as a research prototype. The agent listens to GitHub and other platforms to autonomously open work items, perform tasks, and respond with results such as pull requests, aiming to minimize human attention while maximizing value. The published code is adapted from DeepSeek's internal version and is not production-ready, containing potential bugs and inconsistent engineering practices. Documentation and setup instructions accompany the release, emphasizing the agent's design philosophy and operational principles, with some features planned for future development but not yet implemented.

item.title: Proton senior management shifts to prioritize AI-generated code over security concerns amid internal employee tensions [ ! ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Proton, known for its privacy-focused services like Proton Mail, has shifted from banning AI tools to approving AI for most code development, with about 90% of code reportedly written by AI as of October 2026. This change has raised internal concerns about security testing and employee ability to voice these issues, especially as management emphasizes speed and AI adoption over traditional security practices. The company's CTO, Bart Butler, issued an "AI manifesto" urging engineers to embrace AI fully, framing resistance as a threat to the company's mission. Following an investigation revealing these shifts and employee unease, Proton canceled planned re-interviews tied to AI use that were linked to continued employment, highlighting ongoing internal tensions over AI integration and security priorities.

item.title: Analysis finds AI text watermarking may reduce response diversity and overall quality in multi-turn interactions despite claims of no impact [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Following the EU AI Act's transparency guidelines, major AI labs plan to watermark AI-generated text to indicate provenance. While some claim watermarking does not affect text quality, analysis of Anthropic's Claude model and Google's SynthID-Text method suggests that although single responses maintain quality, watermarking reduces diversity across multiple responses to the same prompt, potentially lowering overall quality in conversational or creative tasks. The watermarking approach swaps random number sequences to embed signals without distorting individual outputs, but this leads to more similar responses in repeated queries, which can hinder creativity and user satisfaction. This trade-off between detectability and diversity raises concerns for typical AI usage scenarios involving iterative prompting and response selection, where inter-response variety is important.

item.title: Anthropic urges Australian government to allow opt-out model for AI training on copyrighted content amid public broadcaster concerns
item.description: Anthropic has called on the Australian government to permit conditional approval for AI training on Australian copyrighted works using an opt-out system, after acknowledging it will not receive a blanket copyright exemption. The company highlighted AI's potential economic benefits but also warned of national security and infrastructure risks. Meanwhile, public broadcasters ABC and SBS have criticized AI firms, urging the government to impose strict regulations to protect media organizations and public interest journalism, including requiring AI companies to comply with copyright, defamation, and privacy laws and participate in news bargaining incentives. The ABC and SBS warned that unregulated AI services could accelerate the decline of traditional news media and erode public trust by using news content without permission or compensation. Anthropic proposed using "do not crawl" signals like robots.txt files to respect content creators' preferences, but SBS argued such measures are often ineffective and place undue monitoring burdens on rights holders. The debate continues as a federal parliamentary inquiry prepares for hearings with AI company executives, including Anthropic and OpenAI, to discuss these issues and the future of AI regulation in Australia.

item.title: The Pragmatic Engineer explores how AI writing most code is reshaping software engineering roles, skills, and development practices in 2026 [ * ] [ ◼ ]

It highlights recent advances in AI models like Opus 4.5, GPT-5.2, and Claude Code that have enabled developers to produce production-ready code with minimal manual input, changing how engineers work and collaborate. It discusses the evolving value of software engineering skills, noting that while traditional coding expertise may decline in importance, roles emphasizing product-mindedness and technical leadership are becoming more critical. The piece also addresses challenges such as increased software complexity, potential quality issues, and shifting boundaries between product management and engineering as AI tools become more capable.

item.title: Developer releases bootgpt, a 512-byte boot sector neural network that simulates a Linux boot log on 386 PCs without an OS [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Bootgpt is a tiny neural network implemented entirely in a 512-byte master boot record (MBR) that loads an 11.5 KB int8 model from adjacent disk sectors and runs in 16-bit real mode on a 386 processor. It generates a fake Linux boot log with timestamps and hardware events, all without an operating system or runtime environment. The project includes assembly code for loading and running the model, Python scripts for training and quantizing the network, and instructions for running it on BIOS-based machines or emulators like QEMU. The model uses a single hidden layer and limited context to produce plausible but synthetic boot messages, leveraging repetition in real boot logs to appear coherent. The entire runtime fits within the MBR, while weights and vocabulary data reside in the following sectors. Bootgpt builds on a tradition of complex programs fitting into boot sectors, with prior examples including chess engines, BASIC interpreters, and transformer models running during boot. This project demonstrates extreme code size optimization and creative use of legacy PC boot processes.

This development highlights the broader challenges social media and content platforms face as AI technologies reshape online traffic patterns and monetization strategies.

Such flagging is applied in contexts like academic integrity checks, content moderation, and authenticity verification to distinguish human-written content from AI-generated text.

item.title: Critical Software restructures around AI with layoffs to boost agility and shift software development for aviation and automotive sectors [ * ] [ ◼ ]
item.description: Critical Software, a technology company based in Coimbra, is fundamentally restructuring its operations around artificial intelligence, leading to layoffs as it adapts to AI-driven software development. Co-founder Gonçalo Quadros explained that routine tasks and code production have increasingly been automated by AI, prompting the company to refocus on critical systems in aviation, aerospace, and automotive sectors that still require human verification. Quadros highlighted that AI has significantly increased productivity, potentially enabling the company to develop technology ten times faster and make previously uneconomical systems viable. While embracing AI, he also expressed concerns about the risks of uncontrolled AI self-improvement, suggesting the company is navigating both opportunities and challenges in this transition.

Despite the clear strategy, the company faces significant internal resistance, fear, and pushback from employees, which has slowed progress and contributed to underperformance against revenue targets. Proton's leadership has taken a hard stance on accelerating AI adoption, including monitoring AI code usage and discouraging traditional testing practices, creating a culture of fear among engineers. This situation highlights that while AI tools can streamline technical tasks, human factors remain the primary challenge in adopting AI-driven workflows effectively.

item.title: Apple CEO John Ternus says the company aims to integrate AI meaningfully rather than 'ship AI for AI's sake'
item.description: Apple CEO John Ternus defended the company's approach to artificial intelligence in a recent interview, emphasizing that Apple plans to leverage AI in its products only when it enhances user experience rather than using AI as a feature on its own. Ternus acknowledged that while Apple has faced criticism for being behind in AI, particularly with delays in upgrading Siri, he is confident in the company's current direction and product strategy. Ternus also addressed the potential impact of AI on Apple's ecosystem, suggesting that while AI could simplify tasks, the creation of products remains a deeply human and personal endeavor for the company. He highlighted that Apple's focus is on building products that users love, regardless of whether AI or traditional software powers them.

item.title: Judge allows NAACP lawsuit against xAI over unpermitted gas turbines at Colossus data center to proceed, rejecting dismissal motion [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: A federal judge denied xAI's motion to dismiss an NAACP lawsuit alleging the SpaceX-owned AI company operated at least 35 combustion turbines at its Colossus data center near Memphis without required air permits, violating the Clean Air Act. The judge ruled that the turbines are not exempt as mobile sources and affirmed the plaintiffs' standing under the Clean Air Act. The NAACP, represented by the Southern Environmental Law Center, has pursued the case to hold xAI accountable for pollution impacting local communities. The decision follows a similar denial of a dismissal motion from the Department of Justice and occurs amid growing public and governmental scrutiny of data center environmental impacts, including recent moratoriums on new data centers in some states.

item.title: Parameter Labs details exploit to take over ChatGPT accounts via sandboxed iframe vulnerability, OpenAI patches issue and pays $5,000 bug bounty [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
item.description: Parameter Labs discovered a complex exploit in ChatGPT's HTML preview feature that allowed untrusted code in sandboxed iframes to execute JavaScript and access private user data. The vulnerability involved the MathLive library's virtual keyboard and a flaw in message handling that enabled injection of unauthorized HTML and scripts through YouTube's oEmbed endpoint. OpenAI responded by closing the security hole and awarding a $5,000 bug bounty for the finding. The exploit could have allowed attackers to create share URLs that, when visited by signed-in users, exfiltrated private data or performed actions on their behalf, highlighting the importance of strict sandboxing and content security policies in interactive web applications.

item.title: Analysis: US and Chinese AI firms adopt divergent models with open-weight Chinese LLMs challenging US tech dominance and complicating AI as an economic weapon [ * ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Since World War II, the US has leveraged its global tech companies to advance national security, but the rise of AI models introduces new dynamics as US and Chinese firms compete with different approaches. US companies like OpenAI keep their best AI models closed and proprietary, while leading Chinese firms openly share model weights, enabling broader access and use. This divergence is fragmenting the AI market into a commoditized tier dominated by open models and a premium tier of closed models, weakening US leverage through technology exports. Chinese open-weight models, though generally less capable than US closed models, are sufficiently effective for many routine tasks, leading businesses and consumers to adopt a mix of open and closed AI services. Market data shows open Chinese models processing a majority of AI usage tokens but accounting for a smaller share of spending, reflecting a split similar to the generic versus branded drug market. This trend suggests that the US's traditional strategy of using proprietary technology as an economic and geopolitical tool may face limits in the evolving AI landscape.

item.title: Ethan Mollick argues individuals have agency to adapt and coexist with AI amid job displacement fears [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: Ethan Mollick, associate professor at Wharton and author of Co-Existence: The Next Phase of AI, discusses how people can navigate the growing presence of AI in work and daily life. Despite widespread anxiety about AI replacing jobs, Mollick emphasizes the importance of using AI tools to understand and integrate them rather than resisting the technology. Mollick highlights recent advances in AI agents that can perform complex tasks with less supervision, increasing productivity across fields. He suggests that while AI poses challenges, individuals have the ability to shape how the technology fits into their lives and careers, advocating for a proactive approach to coexistence with AI rather than fear or denial.

item.title: The Billionaire Tax Might Fail-For Now
item.description: Welcome, Weekenders! Next Tuesday promises to be something of a doozy. At the moment, the Democrats are poised to take back both the Senate and the House of Representatives and clean up nicely in gubernatorial races across the country. And for those of you in California who haven't decamped to the pine-studded shores of Nevada's Incline Village, we'll find out whether you'll need to find a good financial planner. Or a sharkish attorney. Yes, Tuesday is billionaire tax judgment day, with California voters getting a chance to decide on Proposition 40, the ballot proposal that hopes to enact a one-time 5% tax on billion-dollar fortunes to fund healthcare and education in the state. The plan has caused great agita among the tech elite. And while I can't imagine a tremendous number of the people reading this newsletter would favor the proposal, I suggest anyone on the fence-or already in support-should read what Rippling founder Parker Conrad has been saying on X to understand exactly why the idea seems somewhat harebrained. The outcome looks tight. While polls from earlier this year showed fairly strong support for Prop 40, more recent ones suggest voters have turned more negative on the idea. A fresh poll by Politico found 45% of likely voters in favor, 43% against it and 12% undecided. Prediction-market traders take a dim view of Prop 40's odds. Polymarket scores just 23% in favor, while Kalshi shows just about the same. Granted, prediction markets weren't great leading indicators lately for election results in Brazil and Israel. The weakening support among voters comes after a slew of Democratic-aligned groups and trade unions have voiced opposition to Prop 40, including Planned Parenthood, the California Teachers Association and the California Medical Association. Those organizations have varied criticisms of Prop 40-one being that they think state lawmakers won't actually get the money to healthcare and education. California Gov. Gavin Newsom has also said he opposes Prop 40. Should Prop 40 fail, it'll be a victory for the Sergey Brins and Patrick Collisons of the world, who've spent months campaigning against the proposal and committing enormous sums of money to ads and other measures to defeat it. The best-funded group dedicated to torpedoing Prop 40 is Building a Better California, which itself has raised $330 million from Brin, Stripe's Collison, former Google CEO Eric Schmidt, venture capitalist Vinod Khosla and Kleiner Perkins' John Doerr, among many others. And even if Prop 40 passes, both supporters and opponents expect a lengthy series of court battles over its constitutionality. Prop 40 has been a constant matter of discussion in the conversations that Cooper Teboe, an indefatigable Democratic operative in California, has with wealthy donors. "It comes up 20 times a day," he said. "Folks really, really care about it." The prospect of Prop 40's approval has led some wealthy Californians to hesitate to make political donations to Democrats at a time when the newly reascendant party might hope to bring the tech elite back into the fold. "It has made some of them throw up their arms and just say 'Fuck it' to the Democrats," Teboe said. "I've heard from a few people who have stopped giving money because they're like, 'OK, this wealth tax thing is going to wipe me out. I'm going to save every single dollar I can for this tax.'" Even if Prop 40 fails, Teboe believes its mere existence is a harbinger of things to come and expects to see similar measures pop up around the country over the next few years. Teboe finds that many of the donors seem disconnected from the general unease most Americans feel about the state of the economy-a discontent over high inflation and the uncertainty of AI's impact on jobs. The most contact those donors have with more ordinary mortals, Teboe said, is in "the conversations that they have with staff on the way to their Porsche."-Abram Brown (abe@theinformation.com) The Information's Must-Read Stories Can AI Help Ray Kurzweil Cheat Death? Why Publishers Are Adding Invisible Ads for AI Agents How Instacart Ended Up in DoorDash's Cart OpenAI, a Longtime Nvidia Customer, Plans to Buy Google's AI Chips Listening: "Midnight Radio" Actor Ethan Hawke has enjoyed several good cinematic outings with screenwriters Scott Derrickson and C. Robert Cargill, who penned the scripts for "The Black Phone" and "The Black Phone 2," horror films that starred Hawke. (Derrickson and Cargill also wrote "Sinister.") The trio has reunited for "Midnight Radio," a fictional podcast that borrows from the sensibilities of "The Twilight Zone" and "The X-Files." Hawke is the unnamed host of a late-night radio show dedicated to exploring conspiracy theories and the supernatural. He's been at it for some time, and while he still has a devoted fanbase, he seems a bit bored by his program-that is, until a man who claims to be a former U.S. astronaut calls up Hawke's character with a whopper of a story: He and another astronaut actually beat the Russians as the first people to orbit the Earth. Only one of them returned home, a journey that involved interdimensional travel. But why is he suddenly revealing his saga on air to a podunk AM jockey? According to the former astronaut, it's because he's recently decoded a series of secret messages hidden in radio broadcasts that identified the geographical coordinates of the station from which Hawke's character broadcasts. The story's events unfold in real time-keeping the tension high-and Hawke is joined in the cast by Vincent D'Onofrio, Noah Centineo and Hawke's son, Levon.-Abram Brown Reading: "Princes and Thieves" by Matthew Cole Last week, attorneys for Jared Kushner, the Trump son-in-law who serves as one of America's top Middle East envoys, threatened to sue journalist Matthew Cole over an early excerpt from "Princes and Thieves," Cole's account of Kushner's role in the first Trump administration. The excerpt contained an explosive allegation-that Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates had placed $2 billion in bank accounts for Kushner during Donald Trump's initial presidency, part of a broader conspiracy between Kushner and the Arab royals to influence U.S. foreign policy and remake the Middle East. In response to the legal threat, the book's publisher released "Princes and Thieves" several days early. Cole's details about Kushner's alleged schemes will make your mouth hang open. (Kushner denies it all.) Here's just some of what Cole says happened: The money deposited in the accounts came after a 2016 meeting between Kushner and the Emiratis at the Four Seasons hotel in Manhattan, a discussion in which the Emiratis laid out their keen interest in working with the incoming Trump White House. (Relations had been chilly with President Barack Obama.) After Kushner later met with the Emiratis and the Saudis to discuss their grievances against Qatar, the two countries began their yearslong blockade of that country; in their minds, Kushner had given them a tacit greenlight. The blockade ended in 2021-just as Qatar struck a secret deal to financially rescue a New York office tower owned by Kushner's father. In addition, the Arab money channeled to Kushner was partly dispensed to Erik Prince, the Blackwater founder, who attempted to arm a Libyan warlord, among other things.Kushner is one of two principal characters in "Princes and Thieves." The other is Sheikh Mohamed bin Zayed Al Nahyan (aka MBZ), the Emirati ruler. The sheikh loves a scheme-take how he ascended the throne by discrediting his older half-brother and revealing his sibling's gay affairs to their father. (The UAE does not follow strict primogeniture.) Later, MBZ struck up a close relationship with his counterpart in Saudi Arabia, Prince Mohammed bin Salman, coaching the Saudi royal through his own ruthless climb. What both men wanted most was to neuter Iran, which they see as a grave threat. Sometimes MBZ roped Israel into his efforts against Iran, and Israel's central bank administered one of the bank accounts for Kushner. Kushner himself, of course, is deeply interested in Israel and tried to arrange a deal between Israel and the Palestinians during the first Trump administration. "Jared wanted the Gulf royals to support his attempt to force the Palestinians into a deal with Israel," Cole writes. "In return, the Gulf royals wanted aggressive U.S. policy on Iran." The money in the bank accounts provided to Kushner "would grease the wheels." Cole does not know precisely what happened to all the money in the accounts earmarked for Kushner. Nor does he know how much Trump knew about Kushner's actions. And while his reporting for "Princes and Thieves" largely concludes with Trump's departure from office in 2021, Cole casts a spotlight on the obvious specter that hangs over the current Trump White House: Kushner has returned to the Middle East in a role with no congressional oversight-just as Trump has provoked a war with Iran. Such an outcome seems exactly what MBZ would've wanted.-A.B. Watching: "Below" On a remote island off Canada's coast, the residents of Snook's Arm, the fictional setting of this new Netflix series, are barely scraping by. The authorities want them to relocate-but some locals are holding out, including the rather weathered-looking Calvin Penney (Josh Hartnett), who makes a living scooping up chunks of glacial ice and selling them to the one thriving business in town, a vodka distillery that has won a little fame for making its liquor from genuine, melted-down icebergs. When he hauls in a smelly block of frozen matter that the distillery won't buy, he takes it over to a local scientist (Mackenzie Davis), who quickly discovers-eek-it's not ice but a giant hunk of mucus membrane. Penney's not quite sure what to make of that revelation, and besides, he's got other things on his mind, like trying to convince his daughter, Mary (Ruby Stokes), to return home and hold onto his ne'er-do-well son Wade (Charlie Heaton from "Stranger Things"). A third Calvin offspring, Jay (Rohan Campbell), is in his own share of trouble. "Below" has a pleasant, winky off-kilteredness to it, a tone that reminded me a little of Apple's "Widow's Bay," another horror-comedy mashup about the strange happenings on a weird island-though, yes, it is impossible to imagine Snook's Arm ever becoming the next Martha's Vineyard. The show moves fast: By the end of the first episode, a giant mass of tentacles has already ripped apart one of Calvin's iceberg-hunting rivals. (Yeah, gross.) With all the melted ice bobbing around, "Below" is determined to have something to say about the world's climate crisis. Hartnett's innate appeal and the presence of that fearsome beastie from, uh, below keep it quite entertaining.-A.B.

item.title: dbreunig/nesformer [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
item.description: dbreunig/nesformer Inspired by qwenputer by Divyansh Agrawal, Drew Breunig baked a working emulator for a Nintendo Entertainment System 6502 CPU into the weights of Qwen3.5-4B. You can now play NES ROMs such as Super Mario Bros (very slowly) running inside Qwen! In a comment on Hacker News Drew reveals the Opus 5.5 prompts he used to build this system: Read this article and any relevant source code: https://divagr.com/blog/qwenputer. Then explore if you could emulate the chip and ram in a Nintendo Entertainment System (as people do today with FPGAs in MISTRs) using this technique. If so, what size model would you have to build and if you could use smaller faster ones, could you get it to be at the standard clockspeed. Followed by: I think we should build it! Just for fun. It's okay if it's not fast. We want to be able to have the weights, and a cli to run them that we can point at a ROM. Apparently Opus found and then used this collection of conformance tests for the NES CPU released 15 years ago by Christopher Pow. Via Hacker News Tags: games, ai, generative-ai, llms, drew-breunig, qwen, conformance-suites
